subject: Stan 2.0.1 returns "no acceptably small step size could be found"; Stan 1.3.0 ok

messages.author: 0001c090d17a225a
messages.subject: Stan 2.0.1 returns "no acceptably small step size could be found"; Stan 1.3.0 ok
parts:
Dear List,

I returned today to a model I estimated some time back in Stan 1.3.0, thinking I would check the results in Stan 2.0.1 before going on to do some additional analysis. To my surprise, I was immediately greeted with following error when estimating the model in 2.0.1:

  Error : No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?
  error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

The model can be found at following list thread:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/qeMsZMW2bEg/IDeybYvWctUJ

I have searched through the list, and found this error pop up a few times, but none of threads seemed to provide a clear reason why this model would work in 1.3.0 and not in 2.0.1. I have tried to play with the priors and a few other things, but nothing seems to work. I am now concerned that my initial estimates done in 1.3.0 may be suspect. Suggestions?

Thank you,
~Jason

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan 2.0.1 returns "no acceptably small step size could be found"; Stan 1.3.0 ok
parts:
Are you using the same initialization? If you can verify
it works in 1.3 but fails in 2.0.1 with the same initialization
value, I'll file an issue and look into it more deeply.

That error arises when the sampler can't move from
the initial parameter values. Usually this happens
because of an error such as providing out-of-support
inputs to a distribution (e.g., 1.2 ~ beta(1,1)) or
because of NaN values introduced as arguments, such as
dividing 0 by 0. It can also arise due to overflow
or underflow issues.

One issue with your model is:

pos_raw[n-3,K] ~ normal(0, 4);

This only supplies a prior for a single entry in the pos_raw
matrix. If you want all of pos_raw to get this prior, you need
to write:

for (n in 1:(n-3))
pos_raw[n] ~ normal(0,4);

or more efficiently given that n >> K and that
pos_raw is a matrix (stored in column-major order), use:

for (k in 1:K)
col(pos_raw,k) ~ normal(0,4);

Otherwise, you get an implicit uniform prior on the declared
support, which is (-10,10).

To deal with arithmetic stability for the Poisson, we
have a poisson_log() distribution, which takes its parameter
on the log scale and lets you replace:

y ~ poisson(exp(beta - D));

with

y ~ poisson_log(beta - D);

- Bob

Are you using the same initialization?  If you can verify
it works in 1.3 but fails in 2.0.1 with the same initialization

I have confirmed that the model works for 1.3.0 and fails with 2.0.1. I have attached an R script for replication (the code includes fake data generation and can simple be run with source()).

That error arises when the sampler can't move from
the initial parameter values.  Usually this happens
because of an error such as providing out-of-support
inputs to a distribution (e.g.,  1.2 ~ beta(1,1)) or
because of NaN values introduced as arguments, such as
dividing 0 by 0.  It can also arise due to overflow
or underflow issues.

This is what I gathered from some of the other discussions on the mailing list. Nothing jumps out at me as being a problem in my model, but I am not sure how to go about troubleshooting it in more detail.

One issue with your model is:

     pos_raw[n-3,K] ~ normal(0, 4);

This only supplies a prior for a single entry in the pos_raw
matrix.  If you want all of pos_raw to get this prior, you need
to write:

   for (n in 1:(n-3))
     pos_raw[n] ~ normal(0,4);

or more efficiently given that n >> K and that
pos_raw is a matrix (stored in column-major order), use:

   for (k in 1:K)
     col(pos_raw,k) ~ normal(0,4);

Wow, thanks for this. Not sure why I never noticed it before. I guess I just expected the draws from the prior be to vectorized in all dimensions. This may explain some of my convergence issues I've had in larger models. In the attached code, I drop the prior specification so as to eliminate as many variables as possible. But the model still failed in 2.0.1 when I tried to specify them.

Otherwise, you get an implicit uniform prior on the declared
support, which is (-10,10).

To deal with arithmetic stability for the Poisson, we
have a poisson_log() distribution, which takes its parameter
on the log scale and lets you replace:

  y ~ poisson(exp(beta - D));

with

  y ~ poisson_log(beta - D);

I should have mentioned, I did make this change in response to your earlier suggestion.

parts:
I can't keep the names associated with the threads, but
if this is about the standard deviation, the solution was
to code a gradient for the sd() function by hand. It has
a simple form once the dust clears (see the manual). Doing
the algebra allows you to sidestep the (0 / 0) that you get
from blindly applying the chain rule.

- Bob
